Asked Saturday in Florida how far along a possible attack was, he said, according to Middle East Eye and Al Jazeera's live coverage: "Do you really think I'd tell you that. Maybe tomorrow... There's a possibility I will. There's also a possibility we'll have a nice, big, beautiful agreement. They want to make a deal, but the problem is, will they hold the deal?" That directly undercuts his October 8 pledge not to attack Iran before the November 3 midterms — a reversal his critics noted and his supporters framed as keeping Tehran guessing. US Ambassador to Turkey Tom Barrack went further on Friday, telling podcaster Mario Nawfal that a strike "this weekend" was possible, while Trump himself responded that he knew nothing about Barrack's remark — a public split inside the administration's messaging.

The third strand is quieter but arguably more telling: preparation. CNN reported Friday, citing multiple sources and a State Department official, that the US is quietly moving some diplomats and family members out of posts in Lebanon, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar and Jordan as concern grows over further regional escalation. Axios reported an October 23 intelligence memorandum to Secretary of State Marco Rubio, confirmed by a US official to the Jerusalem Post, warning that Iran has substantially increased efforts to target American personnel, with some plots at advanced stages. And the Wall Street Journal reported from aboard the USS George Washington on Sunday that the carrier is rearming in preparation for possible strikes on Iran — a report carried in summary form, with no figures on munitions or any timeline, so it reads as readiness signalling rather than a strike order.

Iran's side of the argument, meanwhile, is that Washington derailed the talks. President Masoud Pezeshkian said on state television that negotiations over an interim agreement were under way before "the cowards (Americans) messed everything up," while still saying Iran should go and conclude a deal. Iran's armed forces chief, Major General Ali Abdollahi, said Saturday that US warships would not be allowed back into the Persian Gulf under any circumstances. And an IRGC-affiliated outlet on Sunday rejected reports that Tehran had offered, via a Pakistani mediator, to reopen the Strait of Hormuz in exchange for lifting the US naval blockade — a reminder that even the supposed diplomatic off-ramps are disputed. Regional voices weighed in against fresh strikes: Egypt, Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan warned that renewed attacks would deepen regional instability, according to Arab News and the Times of Israel, while European and Middle Eastern ministers urged diplomacy instead.

For ordinary people, the stakes are the ones already visible in their bills and travel plans: any fresh strike risks another round of Hormuz disruption and higher fuel prices, Gulf governments are already warning their own citizens and visitors, and the US State Department has updated travel advisories for Saudi Arabia, Qatar, the UAE, Bahrain, Iraq, Lebanon and Israel, citing potential Houthi threats. None of that is abstract for Gulf residents — it is airport alerts, rerouted flights and a risk premium on everything shipped through the strait.

In short: Sunday's threatened strike did not materialise, but the ingredients for one — a claimed drone shootdown, an intelligence warning about targeting US personnel, diplomats quietly leaving posts, and a carrier rearming — all moved in the same 48 hours, while both Trump and Pezeshkian kept talking about a deal neither side seems able to close.

!President Donald Trump speaking, in a photo carried with reporting on his warning of possible fresh strikes on Iran-1792920766858_v.webp)

Caption: President Donald Trump, whose Saturday remarks — a strike on Iran "maybe tomorrow" or a "big, beautiful" agreement — set the tone for Sunday. The deadline passed without a reported strike, but the warning itself, plus the claimed drone shootdown and the diplomat movements, is what moved markets and Gulf travel advice over the weekend.

item.title: Ukraine: no new daytime barrage — but a new wrinkle in the Starlink argument
item.description:
No major new daytime strike wave was reported in Ukraine on Sunday beyond the overnight barrage already covered in the morning brief.
The one new detail comes from CNN's Starlink reporting: Trump said he asked Elon Musk to lift restrictions on Kyiv's military-grade Starlink/Starshield service, while Trump and his top officials denied making the call to throttle it in the first place — and Musk said the administration was behind the ban in a social media post last week. Ukraine's defence ministry says restored speeds above 400 km/h are now being recorded.
In other words, all three parties now agree speeds are back, but nobody agrees on who restricted them or why — the same dispute the morning brief flagged, now with each side's version on the record. Watch Tuesday, October 27, for the Oleshky local ceasefire.

item.title: Sweet Security Research Identifies Go Implementation of Node2Shell Vulnerability, Expanding Attack Surface to Major HTTP Frameworks
item.description:
The Brotli flaw behind Node2Shell is not C-only: Sweet Security found a parallel fix pushed to Go's Brotli library on October 23, confirming the same vulnerability class in Go. That pulls Traefik (direct dependency, Compress middleware), Fiber (via fasthttp) and Iris into scope — combined adoption over 130,000 GitHub stars, Traefik alone over a billion Docker pulls. Sweet Security cautions that dependency presence alone does not prove exploitability — version, encoder-vs-decoder use and configuration matter — but says Go HTTP services decoding client-controlled Brotli input should be inventoried now. This extends the Node.js Brotli fixes already reported October 22; it is not a new KEV entry. Source: GlobeNewswire / Sweet Security.
Watch Monday: CISA KEV federal patch deadlines land October 26 for Nextcloud Collabora (CVE-2026-110447) and Arista VeloCloud (CVE-2026-114625), both already reported and actively exploited.
Source: globenewswire.com.

item.title: A night of drones on both sides — and a public fight over Starlink
item.description:
Russia fired 153 Shahed-type drones at Ukraine overnight into Sunday, including 92 faster jet-powered variants, along with low-cost Banderol cruise missiles, according to Ukraine's Air Force as reported by the Kyiv Independent. Ukraine said it neutralized 119 of the 153 drones, with debris and impacts recorded at 15 locations. The human toll is still being reconciled across reports: the Kyiv Independent-based tally puts 8 people killed and 51 wounded across Ukraine over the past day, while other Sunday reports cite at least 4 killed and 32 injured. A drone hit a residential building in Vinnytsia, injuring six; in Synelnykove, Dnipropetrovsk region, a strike on an apartment building killed four people, including victims who later died in hospital, and injured at least 13, including an 11-year-old girl. In Kharkiv, Russian forces first struck a home-improvement hypermarket, then hit the emergency crews who arrived — a double-tap strike that injured first responders and destroyed a fire engine tanker.
Russia reported its own casualties from Ukrainian strikes. Belgorod's governor said an overnight Ukrainian drone attack on the city killed two people and injured 13, damaging 30 apartment blocks, and another person was killed near Shebekino. In Bryansk region, a drone attack on a minibus belonging to an agricultural enterprise killed two and seriously injured two more. Russia's Defence Ministry said its forces struck Ukrainian logistics centres, port infrastructure and a dry-cargo vessel it claimed was carrying supplies for Ukraine's armed forces near Chornomorsk, and claimed 532 Ukrainian drones were intercepted over 25 Russian regions overnight. Reuters noted it could not independently verify the ministry's claims, and the same caveat applies to both sides' tallies.
The two sides also fought publicly over the satellite link Ukrainian forces depend on. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk wrote on X that Ukraine's military violated Starlink's terms of service by using the civilian service for offensive drone strikes to "kill people," and said that "loophole was closed last week" — a statement that, if it refers to the speed restrictions Ukrainian officials complained about for weeks, would explain them. Ukrainian presidential adviser Serhiy Beskrestnov pushed back, saying commercial Starlink terminals are technically incapable of supporting long-range strikes because of active speed restrictions. Meanwhile Kyiv says Starlink/Starshield access has been restored to full speeds, improving drone command-and-control — a claim that sits uneasily next to Musk's post, and neither side has fully explained the sequence.
President Zelensky used the overnight toll to press his case for air defence. In a Sunday post he said Russia launched around 1,600 guided aerial bombs, 48 missiles and nearly 2,300 attack drones over the past week, hitting a thermal power plant, substations, coal mines, grain storage, shopping malls and a postal logistics hub across nine regions. "This is how Russia responds to diplomacy and deisolation," he wrote, urging European partners to unblock already-approved Patriot interceptor deliveries and keep supporting Ukrainian combat aviation against jet-powered Shaheds.
For ordinary Ukrainians, the pattern is now the war itself: apartment blocks, shops and warehouses hit nightly, emergency crews targeted while responding, and winter approaching with the power grid already under strain. The Oleshky local ceasefire — the one agreed pause in weeks — is still set for Tuesday, October 27, but nothing in the overnight exchange suggests the wider war is slowing for it.
In short: both sides traded heavy drone strikes overnight with civilians killed on both sides of the border, the casualty counts differ by outlet and remain unverified, and the Starlink dispute has moved from quiet restrictions into an open argument between Musk and Kyiv over what the system may be used for.
Sources:
Source: americastrikes.com.

item.title: Riyadh airport reopens its first terminals as the coalition says it stopped 10 missiles
item.description:
King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh reopened Terminals 1 and 2 on Sunday, the first sign of normal operations returning after two weeks in which the airport was repeatedly targeted — including the October 10 strike that killed 13 people and wounded more than 300. The Houthis immediately called the reopened airport a "military target" and warned it is not safe for airlines, employees or travellers, renewing the evacuation warning they have issued since the airport campaign began.
The reopening came under fire. The Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted a ballistic missile and a drone over Riyadh overnight, destroyed a Houthi cruise missile aimed at Khamis Mushait on Sunday morning, and shortly before noon said it had intercepted and destroyed ten Houthi ballistic missiles aimed at the Southern Region. No casualties were linked to the latest interceptions in coalition statements, and there was no independent confirmation of damage from the Houthi side's claims. The Houthis had claimed seven operations on Saturday, including strikes on Riyadh and Dammam airports, Yanbu Aramco facilities, the Rabigh refinery and the East-West pipeline — claims Saudi authorities have not confirmed for the oil sites.
The two narratives have barely moved all month, and that is the story: the coalition reports interceptions and counts no hits; the Houthis claim hits on airports and energy sites and count no need for Saudi confirmation. What changed Sunday is the airport itself — Riyadh is testing whether partial reopening is sustainable while missiles are still being fired at it, and the Houthis are testing whether they can keep that bet from paying off. Egypt's parliament is due to resume its session on Saudi defence authorisation on Monday, October 26, a vote that could formalise more regional backing for the coalition.
For travellers and for the region's economy, the stakes are concrete: Riyadh's airport is the kingdom's main gateway, its closure has already forced airlines to suspend or reroute Gulf services for weeks, and every intercepted missile over the capital keeps the risk premium on Gulf aviation and shipping where it is. If Terminals 1 and 2 stay open through the week, that is a genuine de-escalation signal; if a missile gets through, the closure returns overnight.
In short: Riyadh reopened part of its airport under fire, the coalition says it stopped 11 missiles and drones in a single day, the Houthis say the airport remains a target — and the question of whether civilian aviation can operate through a missile campaign is now being answered in real time.
Sources:
Source: defenseandtech.com.

item.title: Iran / US: post-midterm strike planning reported, no decision confirmed
item.description:
CNN and the New York Times have reported, over October 21–25, that US officials have discussed a short but intense campaign against Iran after the November 3 midterms — roughly three days of strikes on nuclear facilities, energy infrastructure and missile and drone arsenals, coordinated with Israel — while President Trump has publicly pledged not to attack Iran before the midterms and has not confirmed any final decision.
Trump said Saturday the US could take further military action against Iran or reach a deal, without specifying timing. Treat this as reported planning, not a decision: the White House has said it does not comment on military plans "that may or may not exist," and Trump has repeatedly vetoed proposals for a return to major combat this year.
Sources:
Source: suaragarut.id.

item.title: Houthis open a second front in Aden as Saudi strikes kill up to 16 in Yemen
item.description:
The Houthis struck Yemen's interim capital Aden on Saturday while also firing at targets across Saudi Arabia, opening a second front against the Saudi-backed government on its own territory. Yemen's Interior Ministry said two missiles hit the coast guard headquarters inside the ministry's compound and a third struck a coast guard building in the Tawahi district, according to the state-run Saba news agency. Separately, Yemen's Transport Ministry said two ballistic missiles hit Aden International Airport, calling it the "fourth such attack this month" and warning of "a threat to the safety of civil aviation." No casualties were reported in Aden, and an Anadolu Agency correspondent heard three explosions across the city.
The two sides describe the Aden strikes differently, and the gap matters. Houthi spokesman Yahya Saree said his forces targeted "Saudi enemy concentrations" at the al-Nasr camp and a naval base in Aden, naming a Saudi brigadier general he said oversaw them. Saree did not mention the airport; the government did not mention al-Nasr camp. Whether they are describing the same impacts under different names or separate strikes is unclear. What is clear is the intent: the Houthis are framing Aden not as Yemen's capital under attack but as a Saudi forward base, while the government treats the coast guard — a force Saudi Arabia has funded and equipped to patrol the Red Sea approach — as its own.
On the Saudi side, the coalition confirmed intercepting three ballistic missiles aimed at Riyadh, Yanbu and Taif, plus a drone in the Eastern Province, and debris fell in Mecca, Jeddah, Taif and Rabigh. Saree claimed far more — eight sites including the Yanbu Aramco facility, the Rabigh refinery, the East-West pipeline, Dammam and Najran airports and Khamis Mushait air base — but Saudi authorities confirmed none of the oil-site hits. The pattern of the last two weeks held: Houthi claims run well ahead of what Riyadh confirms.
The human cost on the other side of the exchange came from Houthi-run Al-Masirah, relayed by AFP: Saudi strikes killed 11 in Sanaa — four in a house and six women and a child at a cement factory's workers' housing — plus five more in a family home in Hodeida, for a reported total of 16. Saudi Arabia has not commented on civilian casualties in Yemen, and independent verification inside Houthi-held territory is effectively impossible, so those figures are one side's account, not confirmed tolls. The Aden strikes follow a pattern this month: the presidential palace on October 15 (5 killed, 16 wounded) and a military coordination site near the airport on October 21, now the coast guard command — each attack picking off a different node of the Saudi-backed government's infrastructure.
For ordinary people, the stakes are aviation and everyday safety: a fourth missile attack this month on Aden's only functioning commercial airport, debris falling across Saudi Arabia's western seaboard including Mecca and Jeddah, and another round of civilian deaths in Sanaa and Hodeida. The GCC secretary-general called the attacks on Saudi Arabia "heinous," but there has been no comparable UN Security Council statement on the Aden strikes.
In short: the Houthis are now fighting on two fronts in a single day — Saudi cities from the south and the Saudi-backed government in Aden from the north — and the war's civilian toll is rising on both sides of the exchange, with the claims on each side still unverified where it matters most.
Sources:
Source: houseofsaud.com.
item.content:encoded:
The Houthis struck Yemen's interim capital Aden on Saturday while also firing at targets across Saudi Arabia, opening a second front against the Saudi-backed government on its own territory. Yemen's Interior Ministry said two missiles hit the coast guard headquarters inside the ministry's compound and a third struck a coast guard building in the Tawahi district, according to the state-run Saba news agency. Separately, Yemen's Transport Ministry said two ballistic missiles hit Aden International Airport, calling it the "fourth such attack this month" and warning of "a threat to the safety of civil aviation." No casualties were reported in Aden, and an Anadolu Agency correspondent heard three explosions across the city.

The two sides describe the Aden strikes differently, and the gap matters. Houthi spokesman Yahya Saree said his forces targeted "Saudi enemy concentrations" at the al-Nasr camp and a naval base in Aden, naming a Saudi brigadier general he said oversaw them. Saree did not mention the airport; the government did not mention al-Nasr camp. Whether they are describing the same impacts under different names or separate strikes is unclear. What is clear is the intent: the Houthis are framing Aden not as Yemen's capital under attack but as a Saudi forward base, while the government treats the coast guard — a force Saudi Arabia has funded and equipped to patrol the Red Sea approach — as its own.

On the Saudi side, the coalition confirmed intercepting three ballistic missiles aimed at Riyadh, Yanbu and Taif, plus a drone in the Eastern Province, and debris fell in Mecca, Jeddah, Taif and Rabigh. Saree claimed far more — eight sites including the Yanbu Aramco facility, the Rabigh refinery, the East-West pipeline, Dammam and Najran airports and Khamis Mushait air base — but Saudi authorities confirmed none of the oil-site hits. The pattern of the last two weeks held: Houthi claims run well ahead of what Riyadh confirms.

The human cost on the other side of the exchange came from Houthi-run Al-Masirah, relayed by AFP: Saudi strikes killed 11 in Sanaa — four in a house and six women and a child at a cement factory's workers' housing — plus five more in a family home in Hodeida, for a reported total of 16. Saudi Arabia has not commented on civilian casualties in Yemen, and independent verification inside Houthi-held territory is effectively impossible, so those figures are one side's account, not confirmed tolls. The Aden strikes follow a pattern this month: the presidential palace on October 15 (5 killed, 16 wounded) and a military coordination site near the airport on October 21, now the coast guard command — each attack picking off a different node of the Saudi-backed government's infrastructure.

For ordinary people, the stakes are aviation and everyday safety: a fourth missile attack this month on Aden's only functioning commercial airport, debris falling across Saudi Arabia's western seaboard including Mecca and Jeddah, and another round of civilian deaths in Sanaa and Hodeida. The GCC secretary-general called the attacks on Saudi Arabia "heinous," but there has been no comparable UN Security Council statement on the Aden strikes.

In short: the Houthis are now fighting on two fronts in a single day — Saudi cities from the south and the Saudi-backed government in Aden from the north — and the war's civilian toll is rising on both sides of the exchange, with the claims on each side still unverified where it matters most.

Sources:

Source: houseofsaud.com — Read the full article

item.title: Oleshky ceasefire firms up for October 27 — and Starlink is back, Ukrainian officials say
item.description:
The local ceasefire both sides agreed to on Friday now has a converging start date, and a second long-running friction point appears to have eased. Kyiv and Moscow both say their forces will stop firing around the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky from October 27 — Russia's General Gerasimov put it at 4 a.m. Moscow time, Ukraine's ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets at 3 a.m. Kyiv time, the same moment — to let aid in and civilians out. The White House statement still says October 29, a discrepancy that has not been resolved, but the two armies that would actually have to hold fire now agree on the 27th. Ukraine's top negotiator says the ceasefire will cover the wider Kherson region and neighbouring areas needed for the operation, and last several days.
The deal was brokered with US First Lady Melania Trump as what her office called the "exclusive intermediary," and the Kremlin credited her with a "significant contribution." Civilian, non-military officials from both countries are to visit residents at home to assess needs, and those who want to leave will be taken to Russia or to Ukraine, their choice. Around 1,700 civilians remain in Oleshky, down from 24,000 before the war, and conditions are dire: mined roads, limited electricity, and, according to a Nobel Peace Prize-winning Ukrainian activist cited by CNN, people eating grass, with the last official food delivery in May. Pope Leo also raised the town with both Putin and Zelensky in the past week.
Separately, the Institute for the Study of War's October 24 assessment says Ukrainian officials are confirming the resumption of unrestricted access to Starlink and Starshield — the satellite system Ukrainian forces rely on for communications and missile warning — after weeks of speed restrictions that Kyiv said disrupted military operations. That is a sharp change from Friday, when Ukrainian officials said the curbs were still in place despite President Trump's claim they had been lifted. No official explanation for the restrictions, or their lifting, has been given.
On the wider war, the diplomatic track also moved: Zelensky said negotiators from Ukraine, Russia and the US agreed to technical-level talks in the first half of November in Abu Dhabi, though a US official later said Abu Dhabi or Switzerland within a couple of weeks. Zelensky said he hopes a leaders' meeting follows, but cautioned that much depends on Russia — a similar meeting expected this month never happened, and Moscow still demands all of Donbas, including territory it does not control, which Kyiv rejects.
For ordinary Ukrainians, the Oleshky deal is narrow — one town, a few days — but it is the first agreed pause either side has confirmed in weeks, and restored Starlink access matters far beyond it: it affects how Ukrainian forces communicate, coordinate and receive warning of incoming missiles. The November talks are the real test of whether a humanitarian opening becomes anything bigger.
In short: both armies now agree the Oleshky guns fall silent October 27, Starlink restrictions appear lifted, and three-way talks are set for early November — modest steps, but the first ones in the same direction in weeks.
Sources:
Source: reuters.com.

item.title: Oil at $117: the US taps its emergency reserve as Hormuz claims go unverified
item.description:
Brent crude briefly topped $117 a barrel on Friday — its highest since the war involving Iran began — and settled at $116.72, with WTI at $103.27, as the Strait of Hormuz shipping crisis kept tightening. The US Department of Energy on Friday authorized an emergency exchange of up to 400,000 barrels from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve for Phillips 66's Lake Charles refinery in Louisiana, to offset a crude delivery disruption. Reuters notes the reserve is already at its lowest since 1982 after the releases tied to the Iran war, and this draw, like the 4-million-barrel hurricane exchange earlier in October, is a loan: Phillips 66 must return more barrels than it borrows.
The price spike is being driven by claims that remain unverified. Iran's Revolutionary Guard said two supertankers carrying more than 4.5 million barrels combined struck naval mines on what Tehran calls an unauthorized southern route, with crews abandoning both vessels — a claim carried by Iranian state media and several regional outlets but confirmed by no maritime authority. President Trump dismissed the claims on Thursday as fabricated to lift oil prices before the November 3 midterms, saying more oil is moving through Hormuz than before the war. Independent monitors split the difference: IMF PortWatch recorded just 4 transits on October 18 against a pre-crisis baseline of 85 per day, while Kpler put total oil flows for the week ending October 18 at 24.5 million barrels per day — roughly pre-war levels, rerouted rather than stopped.
October is already the worst month on record for attacks on commercial shipping in and around the strait, per MarineLink and Reuters, with 28 attacks in the month and 113 since February 28. An Iranian envoy also said Iran remains open to talks with the US under a Pakistan-brokered deal, according to AP — a diplomatic thread running alongside the military one.
For ordinary people, this is already a fuel-price story: diesel prices in Europe have jumped sharply, US fuel markets are leaning on an emergency reserve at 1980s lows, and every unverified mine claim moves the pump price regardless of whether a ship actually sank. The gap between what Tehran claims, what Washington denies, and what shippers can confirm is itself now a market force.
In short: oil is at wartime highs, the US is lending from a depleted emergency stockpile, and the Hormuz shipping war is being fought as much through claims and counterclaims as through actual strikes — watch whether any independent authority confirms a vessel loss, which would be the next real escalation.
Sources:
Source: reuters.com.

item.title: Microduck — a tiny open-source robot duck that walks with reinforcement learning
item.description:
Pollen Robotics' Microduck is a 25 cm, 800 g biped driven by a 50 Hz control loop over 15 servos, with policies trained in simulation (MuJoCo/PPO) and exported to ONNX.
It walks, rolls, picks things up and gets back up when knocked over. The software is Rust, Apache-2.0, and it was trending on GitHub with ~11,000 stars.

Source: digisoulhub.com.

item.title: Capcom breach: 11.7 million CAPCOM ID emails exposed (catch-up, disclosed October 22)
item.description:
Capcom confirmed unauthorized third-party access to its CAPCOM ID membership service, exposing email addresses plus account creation date, last login, login count and last-login IP for 11,774,247 accounts.
For 43 accounts, birth dates, gender, country and nicknames were also exposed, and 196 accounts had passwords changed without authorization (since reset). No credit card data was involved.
Capcom detected the intrusion October 19 and reported it to Osaka police and Japan's privacy regulator October 21. The real risk now is phishing using the leaked emails.
Sources:
Source: beebom.com.

item.title: Houthis claim a coast-to-coast strike wave; Saudis report intercepts over Taif and Yanbu, and Sanaa reports 11 dead in retaliation strikes
item.description:
The Saturday fighting in the Saudi–Houthi war widened from the capital to the Red Sea coast. In a statement carried by the Houthi-run Saba news agency at about 7 PM local time, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree claimed seven missile and drone operations: King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, an Aramco facility in Yanbu, the Rabigh refinery, pumping stations and the East-West crude pipeline, King Fahd International Airport in Dammam, Najran airport, and the air base at Khamis Mushait. Saree claimed every target was hit and that air traffic at Dammam was disrupted. None of that has been independently verified, and Saudi authorities had not confirmed any hits on oil sites at the time of writing, according to Defense and Tech's summary of the day's statements.
What the coalition does confirm is a second wave of intercepts after the morning's Riyadh missile, which was covered in the morning brief. Later Saturday, the coalition said it destroyed two ballistic missiles fired toward Taif and Yanbu, and Saudi Civil Defence briefly issued alerts for Taif, Yanbu, Mecca and Jeddah, lifting them about ten minutes later, Reuters reports via Defense and Tech. Civil Defence said debris from the intercepted missiles fell in Wadi al-Mughammas in Mecca, Jeddah's al-Nuzha district, Wadi Jalil in Taif, and the Mastoura area of Rabigh governorate. No casualties were mentioned in the Civil Defence statement, and it did not address the Houthi claims about Aramco, the pipeline, or the Rabigh refinery.
The two sides tell very different stories about the retaliation. Saree said the strikes were retaliation for what he described as 100 Saudi air strikes on Sanaa and other Houthi-held areas in the previous 24 hours. The Houthi-run Health Ministry in Sanaa said Saudi aircraft hit a house in the capital's Asr area, killing three people and injuring three, and hit workers' housing at a cement factory in Hamdan district, killing eight people — including three women and four children — and injuring 15. Defense and Tech notes it had not seen a coalition statement on those reports. Separately, Yemen's internationally recognised government said three Houthi ballistic missiles hit coast guard sites in Aden, Reuters reports.
Why Yanbu and Rabigh matter: Yanbu, on the Red Sea, is the western end of Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline, which lets the kingdom export crude without sending it through the Strait of Hormuz. Rabigh, on the same coast north of Jeddah, hosts a large refining complex. Any confirmed damage there would matter well beyond Saudi Arabia — which is exactly why the gap between the Houthi claim and the Saudi account matters, and why neither should be taken as confirmed yet. One earlier claim did gain partial Saudi confirmation Saturday: on Thursday, Oct 22, the Houthis claimed attacks on the defence ministry in Riyadh, Aramco facilities in Yanbu, and Dammam airport, and Saudi authorities said two people were killed in Dammam but did not confirm the other two claims, according to Reuters.
In short: Saturday's war of claims stretched from Riyadh to the Red Sea coast, with confirmed intercepts over Taif and Yanbu, unconfirmed Houthi claims of hits on Yanbu, Rabigh and the East-West pipeline, and 11 reported dead in Sanaa from Saudi retaliation strikes. Watch for any Saudi confirmation or denial on the oil sites, and any independent evidence of damage at Yanbu or Rabigh.
Sources:
Source: defenseandtech.com.

item.title: Crimea's blackout is now a rationing regime — power and water restricted, trolleybuses halted, no restoration timeline
item.description:
Saturday brought the first official picture of how bad the Crimea blackout is, and it is worse than a one-night outage. Sergei Aksyonov, the Moscow-installed head of Crimea, said restrictions on electricity and water are now in force across the peninsula after what he called an accident on the main power lines outside Crimea caused by a drone attack. Sevastopol's Russian-installed governor, Mikhail Razvozhaev, said only about 40% of the city's basic mobile-communication base stations are working, trolleybus service has been suspended, and water has been supplied at reduced pressure in parts of Sevastopol's Leninsky district since 9 AM Saturday, with water trucks organised for residents. Social facilities are running on backup power, and Razvozhaev said generator reserves last about four hours before mobile crews recharge them. Kyiv24 reports the timeline for full restoration is currently unknown.
The details behind the blackout are still contested. Monitoring channel Crimean Wind reported a fire at the Taman substation in Russia's Krasnodar Krai, through which all four lines of the Kerch Strait energy bridge run, and NASA FIRMS satellite imagery indicated damage there, according to earlier reporting. Nightwatch's Saturday intelligence summary says Russia's Energy Ministry confirmed new power disruption affecting consumers in occupied Crimea and occupied parts of Kherson, Zaporizhzhia, Donetsk and Luhansk oblasts, but cautions that the Taman fire is corroborated while its connection to the full outage footprint and the extent of physical damage remain unresolved. The Kyiv Independent could not independently verify the extent of the blackouts, and Ukrainian military officials have not commented. For ordinary people, the distinction matters less than the rationing: rolling outages, patchy mobile service, suspended electric transport, and reduced water pressure are now the daily reality until the grid is repaired.
Elsewhere in Ukraine on Saturday, Ukrainian officials said Russian drone and missile strikes across eastern Ukraine killed at least five people, according to Storysh, and a Russian strike on Chernihiv set a disused building ablaze and injured two people, EGazette reports. In Russia, Nightwatch notes imagery supporting fires after UAV activity over Omsk, but says identification of the affected facilities remains preliminary.
In short: Crimea has gone from blackout to rationing — power, water, mobile service and trolleybuses all restricted, with no restoration date — while the exact damage at the Taman substation and its link to the full outage remain unverified. Watch for restoration claims versus renewed blackouts in Simferopol, Yalta and Alushta, which already flickered once after initial restoration claims.
Sources:
Source: kyiv24.com.

item.title: Oleshky — new details on the Oct 27 deal:
item.description:
Reuters, CNN and The Times have now filled in the diplomacy behind the local ceasefire reported in the morning brief.
The deal was brokered with US First Lady Melania Trump acting as what her office calls the "exclusive intermediary," working directly with Ukrainian and Russian leadership; she said Oleshky's remaining 1,700–2,000 residents are mostly elderly in urgent need of medicine, food and clean water, with 30–50 children also thought to be in the town, and that residents who evacuate will get transport to their preferred destination — "some will want to go to Russia, and some to Ukraine." Newsmax says it was granted exclusive TV access to document the operation.
On the wider war, Zelensky said technical-level talks with Russia and the US are set for the first half of November in Abu Dhabi, while a US official later said the next round could be in Abu Dhabi or Switzerland within a couple of weeks. The Oct 27 vs Oct 29 start-date dispute flagged in the morning brief is still unresolved.

Reuters, CNN and The Times have now filled in the diplomacy behind the local ceasefire reported in the morning brief.

The deal was brokered with US First Lady Melania Trump acting as what her office calls the "exclusive intermediary," working directly with Ukrainian and Russian leadership; she said Oleshky's remaining 1,700–2,000 residents are mostly elderly in urgent need of medicine, food and clean water, with 30–50 children also thought to be in the town, and that residents who evacuate will get transport to their preferred destination — "some will want to go to Russia, and some to Ukraine." Newsmax says it was granted exclusive TV access to document the operation.

On the wider war, Zelensky said technical-level talks with Russia and the US are set for the first half of November in Abu Dhabi, while a US official later said the next round could be in Abu Dhabi or Switzerland within a couple of weeks. The Oct 27 vs Oct 29 start-date dispute flagged in the morning brief is still unresolved.

item.title: Hormuz — the oil paradox:
item.description:
Total oil flows actually reached 24.5 million barrels per day in the week ending Oct 18 — slightly above the 24.4 million pre-war average from Feb 22 — according to Kpler data reported by TuzaraPost, because Gulf producers rerouted exports around the strait via the Red Sea and other alternatives.
But traffic through the strait itself is a fraction of normal: about 20 ships a day versus 100+ before the war, with many running dark (transponders off). US Central Command's claim of about 400 merchant transits in the preceding week is far higher than Kpler's count — the gap itself is a measure of how murky the strait picture is.
The IRGC says the strait is closed; CENTCOM says it is open; both can be half-right at once when "open" means a trickle of dark ships. Source:
Source: tuzarapost.substack.com.

item.title: iPhone Duo launch day: lines returned, walk-ins sold out within hours, resales hit $10,000 — and Apple briefly retook the world's most-valuable crown
item.description:
Apple's first foldable had the kind of launch day the iPhone hasn't seen in years. MacRumors reports queues of dozens to hundreds of people at Apple Stores worldwide on Friday, with some lining up a day or two early; Apple's CEO John Ternus and retail chief Deirdre O'Brien greeted customers in Austin, while marketing chief Greg Joswiak did the same at Fifth Avenue in New York, where video showed a massive queue as early as 4:15 AM. Apple had warned walk-in stock would be "limited," and it was: the NY Post reports Fifth Avenue was out of stock for walk-ins by around 10 AM, King of Prussia (Pennsylvania) sold out shortly after 8 AM, and other stores followed within hours. The scarcity fed instant resale markups — eBay listings up to $10,000 for a 2TB Night Sky model against a $3,199 purchase price, and a Craigslist listing at $7,999, per the NY Post.
The launch day also briefly reshuffled the market-cap leaderboard. 9to5Mac reports Apple traded above $351 on Friday, a new intraday record, reaching a market value around $5.12 trillion and retaking the title of world's most valuable company from Nvidia. The lead did not clearly hold: one tracker had Nvidia back ahead by roughly $20 billion at the close, and Ainvest notes the flip was driven mostly by Nvidia's 4.4% fall on Oct 22 in a broad AI-stock sell-off rather than by Duo sales alone — Apple rose only about 1% to its record close. For buyers, the practical takeaway is simpler than the market-cap drama: Duo demand is real, walk-in supply is thin, and Apple had pointed shoppers to a Saturday check of the Apple Store app for pickup availability.
In short: the Duo's launch day combined genuine demand (lines, same-day sellouts) with scalper markups up to 3x retail, and a market-cap crown that Apple grabbed intraday and may not have kept at the close. Watch for restock timing and whether the hinge-crease reports from early owners turn into a real defect pattern.
Sources:
Source: macrumors.com.

item.title: NVIDIA OpenShell — the agent sandbox runtime, trending:
item.description:
OpenShell, Nvidia's open-source runtime for running AI agents safely, hit GitHub trending on Saturday with about 18.7k stars.
It is Apache-2.0, written in Rust, latest release v0.1.5 (Oct 20). Each agent runs in its own kernel-enforced sandbox, every network connection passes a policy check before leaving the sandbox, agents never see real credentials (OpenShell injects them only into requests to approved endpoints), and risky policy changes get flagged by formal verification before a human approves them.
Why it matters: it is the practical answer to "let the agent do things, but not everything" — the same OpenShell name appeared in Nvidia's GTC Berlin reference architecture this week, but this is the runtime itself gaining traction. Sources:
Source: digisoulhub.com.

item.title: PHP2Shell — first confirmed break-in, Palo Alto affected, patch lag now the story:
item.description:
The flaw is no longer just a warning. Palo Alto Networks' Unit 42 reports the first confirmed PHP2Shell compromise, at a European government body, carried out with an AI attack agent, according to Carthage Electronics' Oct 24 threat brief.
Palo Alto confirmed on Oct 24 that the flaws affect its PAN-OS and Panorama management interfaces (product impact rated 8.7, below the underlying PHP 9.2), with no malicious exploitation against its own products known so far — fixed hotfixes are dated Oct 26 (11.1.16-h4) and Oct 28 (12.2.4-h1), with Panorama versions still to be confirmed; until then, restrict management-interface access to trusted addresses only. Meanwhile the patch lag is measurable: more than 21,000 Danish websites still lacked PHP security updates as of Saturday, per Danish industry reporting via NordiskPost, with Denmark's Aula school platform and the Danish Meteorological Institute among precautionary shutdowns (Norway and Finland took similar precautions), and South Africa's Presidency website remained offline as a precaution, with a spokesperson telling Reuters there was no indication of a breach.
Cloudflare's Matthew Prince said exploitation attempts on Cloudflare's network rose from thousands before disclosure to millions after. Most of what researchers see is still scanning, not confirmed mass break-ins — but the first confirmed compromise means the window for "we'll patch Monday" is closing.
Sources:
Source: carthageelectronics.com.

item.title: HPE Aruba — eight CVSS 10.0 flaws, patch this weekend if you run Aruba gear:
item.description:
HPE's advisory HPESBNW05162 (Oct 22) patches 72 vulnerabilities in the ArubaOS systems running wireless networks, and eight carry the maximum CVSS score of 10.0 — authentication bypasses, command injection, SQL injection and buffer overflows letting an unauthenticated attacker run commands on AOS-8 and AOS-10 Mobility Conductors, Controllers, Gateways and Access Points, several via the PAPI access-point management protocol on UDP port 8211.
HPE says it is not aware of exploit code or attacks. Fixed releases: AOS-10 10.8.1.2, 10.7.2.7, 10.4.1.14 and AOS-8 8.13.3.1, 8.10.0.24.
Aruba gear sits in a lot of schools, clinics, warehouses and offices, so this is a weekend-planning item, not a Monday item. Source:
Source: carthageelectronics.com.

item.title: Quest Diagnostics breach confirmed — patient records accessed, scope still unknown:
item.description:
Quest told the SEC (8-K filed Oct 22) that it learned on Oct 21 of unauthorised access to its Quanum Lab Services Manager platform, used by healthcare clients to order lab tests and retrieve results.
Its Oct 23 security notice confirmed protected health information and personally identifiable information were involved, including "personal information and patient records," but the company has not disclosed how many patients are affected, which data types were taken, or when the intrusion began. Clinics relying on Quanum LSM are being told to place orders on paper forms or through Quanum eLabs, per BleepingComputer reporting.
If your doctor sends samples to Quest, this is one to watch — not a reason to panic, but a reason to watch insurance statements and unexpected messages. Sources:
Source: techycluster.com.

item.title: LiteLLM shipped a malicious release — check if you pulled 1.107.0:
item.description:
LiteLLM disclosed on Oct 24 that a master key for its Agent Platform, committed to a public repository on May 27, 2026, sat unrevoked for 136 days and was used from Oct 10 to steal an org owner's GitHub token — ending with a malicious LiteLLM 1.107.0 published to PyPI, Docker Hub and GHCR on Oct 21.
The poisoned PyPI release was live for roughly 1 hour 45 minutes before quarantine; the container tags stayed poisoned for about two and a half hours. Anyone who installed LiteLLM 1.107.0 or pulled the affected container tags on Oct 21 should treat exposed inference keys (Anthropic, OpenAI, AWS Bedrock, Together AI and more, per the report) as compromised and rotate them.
Single-source disclosure report — treat the details as reported, but the remediation advice stands regardless. Source:
Source: dev.to.

item.title: Overnight, both sides hit each other's war machine — and Crimea went dark
item.description:
The overnight exchange was a mirror image: Ukraine says it struck three Russian defence-linked sites, Russia fired 126 drones at Ukraine, and occupied Crimea lost power after a substation attack in southern Russia. None of it touches the narrow Oleshky humanitarian deal, which is still stuck on its own start-date dispute.
The details, in order. According to Reuters, Ukraine's General Staff said its forces hit the Proton-Elektroteks plant in Oryol, the Tolyattikauchuk petrochemical complex in Tolyatti, and an aircraft at the Yeysk airfield in Krasnodar region during operations on October 23 and overnight into Saturday. Kyiv says Proton makes components for cruise and ballistic missiles, and that Tolyattikauchuk's synthetic rubber can go into solid rocket propellant. Tolyatti mayor Ilya Sukhikh confirmed damage at several industrial facilities but did not name them, and reported no deaths or injuries there in preliminary information. At Yeysk, local authorities confirmed an attack but said it caused only minor damage to two apartment buildings — a much smaller account than Kyiv's aircraft-hit claim, so the scale there is unresolved. Separately, Oryol governor Andrei Klychkov said three people were killed Friday in a Ukrainian missile strike on an unspecified civilian facility in the region; Ukraine's General Staff did not report casualties, and the reports do not establish whether the two accounts describe the same strike. Russia's Defence Ministry, for its part, said air defences destroyed 1,297 drones, one French-made SCALP cruise missile and four Ukrainian Neptune missiles over the previous 24 hours — a ministry tally, not an independently verified count.
Russia's overnight barrage, according to Ukraine's Air Force via Anadolu Agency, was 126 drones, of which 101 were shot down, with strikes recorded at 14 locations. In Kyiv, the city military administration said two people were injured after an attack damaged a private residential building in the Obolonskyi district. Kharkiv's mayor reported a drone strike on the city's Industrialnyi district. Russia's Defence Ministry said it struck a facility at the port of Chornomorsk in the Odesa region used for producing uncrewed surface vessels, and a dry-cargo ship it said was carrying supplies for Ukraine's armed forces. In Russia's Rostov region, governor Yury Slyusar said drone debris damaged a transformer substation in the settlement of Kalinin, leaving more than 170 homes without power, and one person was injured.
The Crimea blackout is the night's biggest infrastructure story. According to the Kyiv Independent, via monitoring channels and NASA FIRMS satellite imagery, an attack damaged the Taman substation in Russia's Krasnodar Krai, which supplies occupied Crimea through the Kerch Strait energy bridge. The monitoring channel Exilenova+ reported on the evening of October 23 that "the entire peninsula is without electricity." Sevastopol's Russian-installed governor, Mykhailo Razvozhaev, confirmed on Telegram that the city was without power "as a result of an enemy attack on energy infrastructure outside of Sevastopol." Local authorities later claimed power was restored in multiple cities, but the Crimean Wind channel reported renewed blackouts in Simferopol, Yalta and Alushta, and internet watchdog NetBlocks reported widespread internet outages across the peninsula. Ukraine has not commented on the Taman attack, and the Kyiv Independent could not independently verify the extent of the blackouts. A Kyiv-based outlet separately reported electricity and water restrictions imposed after the blackout, with Sevastopol trolleybus service temporarily suspended.
What each side argues has not moved, but the rhetoric sharpened overnight. In an ABC News interview reported Saturday morning, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy described the Trump administration's recent actions toward Kyiv as "not supportive," and repeated that Starlink and Starshield speed restrictions are still in effect and interceptor-missile supplies are still delayed — directly contradicting President Trump's claim that access was restored. Zelenskyy also took a swipe at US envoy Steve Witkoff, who recently praised Vladimir Putin as "a humanitarian." Separately, the Independent's live blog reports that US lawmakers have written to Elon Musk giving him until October 31 to answer five questions about his control over Ukraine's military communications, warning that personal control over a foreign country's military communications raises corporate-governance and disclosure questions. That letter is reported by the Independent's live blog, not yet confirmed in a standalone report, so treat it as developing. On the Black Sea thread from Friday night, Moldova has now strongly condemned the attack on the civilian vessel near Romania's territorial waters, saying it stands in solidarity with Romania, Ukraine and Azerbaijan and urging a halt to attacks on civilian shipping.
For ordinary people, the Oleshky question is still the one with a human clock on it. Both Kyiv and Moscow now say their forces will stop firing around Oleshky at 4 a.m. local time on October 27 — Ukraine's human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets told the Associated Press the truce starts Tuesday and lasts several days, beginning with demining, then aid deliveries and evacuations — while the White House statement still gives October 29. Until the aid operation itself confirms a date, the roughly 1,700–2,000 mostly elderly residents still there wait. And the Crimea blackout is a reminder that the energy war cuts both ways: Ukrainian cities have lived through this all month, and now Sevastopol, Yalta and Simferopol are reporting the same kind of night.
In short: no breakthrough, no general ceasefire — just a grinding exchange of strikes on defence plants, ports and power grids, a still-unresolved Starlink dispute now drawing congressional questions, and an Oleshky aid operation whose start date Kyiv and Moscow agree on but Washington does not. Watch for whether Crimea's power holds through the weekend, for any Musk response ahead of the October 31 letter deadline, and for which Oleshky date the convoys actually run on.
Reuters, Russia says drone attack damages Togliatti facilities, Ukraine says petrochemical plant hit · Anadolu Agency via Europe Says, Russia, Ukraine trade accusations over overnight strikes · Kyiv Independent via Zotpaper, Mass blackouts hit occupied Crimea after attack on key substation · Independent live blog via Europe Says, Ukraine-Russia war latest · BBC via Today News Brief, Russia and Ukraine agree Oleshky ceasefire
No clean lead image could be retrieved from the Reuters or Kyiv Independent pages this morning, so this article runs without one rather than with a guessed image.
Source: reuters.com.

For ordinary people, the Oleshky question is still the one with a human clock on it. Both Kyiv and Moscow now say their forces will stop firing around Oleshky at 4 a.m. local time on October 27 — Ukraine's human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets told the Associated Press the truce starts Tuesday and lasts several days, beginning with demining, then aid deliveries and evacuations — while the White House statement still gives October 29. Until the aid operation itself confirms a date, the roughly 1,700–2,000 mostly elderly residents still there wait. And the Crimea blackout is a reminder that the energy war cuts both ways: Ukrainian cities have lived through this all month, and now Sevastopol, Yalta and Simferopol are reporting the same kind of night.

In short: no breakthrough, no general ceasefire — just a grinding exchange of strikes on defence plants, ports and power grids, a still-unresolved Starlink dispute now drawing congressional questions, and an Oleshky aid operation whose start date Kyiv and Moscow agree on but Washington does not. Watch for whether Crimea's power holds through the weekend, for any Musk response ahead of the October 31 letter deadline, and for which Oleshky date the convoys actually run on.

item.title: Another missile at Riyadh, and Brent crude tops $117
item.description:
Saturday morning brought another Houthi missile at the Saudi capital and another leg up in oil prices — the two threads of this crisis moving together, as they have all week.
The details first. According to the Saudi-led coalition, via TBS News and AFP, air defences intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by the Houthis toward Riyadh early on Saturday, after civil defence activated an early-warning system for residents in Riyadh, Najran and Wadi al-Dawasir. Two explosions were heard in the capital, an AFP journalist reported. Coalition spokesman Turki al-Malki said a drone was also intercepted in the Eastern Province earlier on Saturday morning. No casualties were reported from the Saturday interceptions. Tehran, for its part, has denied involvement in the Houthi attacks after Saudi Arabia accused Iran of encouraging the escalation — a denial to weigh against the coalition's attribution, which is the standard pattern in this war: coalition claims, Houthi claims, and little independent confirmation of what was hit or missed.
On oil, the numbers are now the story. Brent crude briefly rose above $117 a barrel on Friday, its highest since the war with Iran began in February, and settled at $116.72, with WTI settling at $103.27 — a 22-week high — according to market reporting summarised by ForexRev, drawing on FXStreet and Yahoo Finance data. The immediate trigger, per an Aalimi Nation report from New Delhi, was a new claim from Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps Navy that two supertankers struck naval mines in the southern Strait of Hormuz after using what Tehran calls an "unauthorized route," leaving both vessels disabled with engine-room fires and crews abandoning ship, carrying more than 4.5 million barrels combined. None of that account has been independently confirmed, and it sits alongside the still-unverified Iranian claim of seven tankers hit on October 21–22, which President Trump publicly dismissed as fabricated, saying Iran is inventing hits to lift oil prices before the November 3 US midterms and that more oil is moving through the Gulf than before the war. What is confirmed is the direction of the market and the shipping risk: October is already the worst month on record for Hormuz shipping attacks (28 attacks, per the Reuters/Washington Institute tally reported Friday), war-risk cover for a Gulf transit is being quoted far above pre-war levels, and about a third of crossings now use the northern route under Iranian control, according to Reuters' Ron Bousso.
For ordinary people, this is the fuel-price channel, not an abstraction. Brent above $117 after settling around $112 on October 22 is the kind of move that shows up at pumps and in heating and freight costs within weeks, and it is driven as much by risk pricing and insurance as by any single confirmed sinking. The US ordered non-emergency government staff and families out of Saudi Arabia earlier in the week, and Riyadh's airport is still only partly open — so the practical picture for travellers is unchanged: postpone non-essential trips, and expect airline suspensions to keep rolling forward.
In short: no newly verified Houthi hit on a Saudi target Saturday morning — the missile was intercepted, by the coalition's account — but the oil market is now pricing this crisis at its worst level of the war, and Tehran's unverified tanker claims are doing as much work as confirmed strikes. Watch for any independent confirmation of the two claimed supertanker minings, for Egypt's parliament vote on military support on October 26, and for whether Brent holds above $117 or retreats.
TBS News / AFP, Saudi-led coalition intercepts ballistic missile launched towards Riyadh · Aalimi Nation, Hormuz tanker attacks: Brent crude tops $117 a barrel · ForexRev, Crude oil prices surge to 22-week highs after Gulf attacks
No clean lead image could be retrieved from the TBS or market-report pages this morning, so this article runs without one rather than with a guessed image.
Source: tbsnews.net.

item.title: Nvidia: full order book, uncertain delivery calendar
item.description:
An ad-hoc analysis published Saturday reports ByteDance, Alibaba and Tencent have ordered over 3 million RTX PRO 5500 cards worth $35B+, but that Nvidia cannot guarantee fulfilment as capacity lags — while Nvidia plans 2.5x substrate capacity and a $1.1B KYEC prepayment.
Separately, Nvidia's DSX POD modular reference design for Vera Rubin AI factories, introduced this week, is claimed to cut deployment at prepared sites from six months to as little as 14 days, with partner deliveries planned worldwide for early 2027. Treat both as analyst reporting, not Nvidia guidance: announced, not yet executed.
Source: ad-hoc-news.de.

item.title: VoxCPM2: a 30-language open voice model you can host yourself
item.description:
OpenBMB shipped VoxCPM2, a 2-billion-parameter tokenizer-free text-to-speech model under Apache 2.0: 30 languages with no language tag needed, 48kHz output reconstructed from a 16kHz reference clip, trained on more than 2 million hours of multilingual speech, running in roughly 8 GB of VRAM with a real-time factor near 0.30 on an RTX 4090.
The notable feature is voice design — describe a gender, age, tone and pace in plain language and it invents a voice with no reference audio — and LoRA fine-tuning from as little as 5–10 minutes of audio. The commercial terms are the headline: Apache 2.0, no revenue cap.
Caveat from the write-up itself: voice-design output varies between runs, so generate a few takes.
Source: siliconnoon.com.

item.title: SafePay ransomware has hit 600+ organisations — and it destroys backups first
item.description:
Catch-up, not overnight news: a joint advisory (AA26-293A) from CISA, the FBI, the US Secret Service and German and UK law enforcement, released October 20, says SafePay has compromised at least 600 organisations across critical infrastructure sectors since August 2024, across North America, South America, Europe and Australia.
SafePay is unusual in running as a non-affiliate operation — no outside affiliates, tight operational control. Initial access comes through brute-forced VPN credentials (often via Mullvad VPN exit nodes), phished account profiles, and automated exploitation of five known CVEs on internet-facing devices, including CVE-2024-40711 (CVSS 9.8, Veeam Backup and Replication deserialization).
Once inside, it uses living-off-the-land tools (PsExec, WinRM, RDP), harvests credentials, exfiltrates with 7-Zip/WinRAR and Rclone — and then factory-resets NAS devices, deletes shadow copies and kills backup agent processes before encrypting, so victims have no recovery path. Mitigations: patch those five CVEs, enforce MFA on remote access, and keep backups isolated and offline.
Why it matters now: it was not in this week's briefs, and its backup-destruction playbook is the detail that changes incident planning.
Source: gbhackers.com.

item.title: A certificate authority quit the TLS business after its private keys turned out to be trivially guessable
item.description:
Catch-up: Indian CA eMudhra announced October 22 that its board has voluntarily withdrawn from the global SSL/TLS certificate business, after a researcher showed the private keys behind eight of its browser-trusted intermediate certificates were so weak they could be calculated from the public certificates — one key was literally the number 4, and researcher Scott Helme recovered all eight on a laptop in under a second.
The keys came from a flawed key-generation ceremony in April 2025; Google, Mozilla, Apple and Microsoft blocked the affected certificates between October 17 and 20, and fixes have shipped in Go, Python, Node.js, Java and major Linux distributions. eMudhra says no end-entity certificates were issued from the affected intermediates, its infrastructure was not compromised and no data was breached, and it will keep revocation services running until all issued certificates expire or are replaced — offering Sectigo-issued replacements. Software that never checks revocation remains exposed until updated.
Source: computerworld.com.

item.title: Diplomacy on paper, drones over Moscow, and a ship hit off Romania
item.description:
Friday evening's war news undercut the day's diplomacy in three directions at once: Ukrainian drones shut down Moscow's airports for the second time in two days, a likely Russian drone struck a cargo ship just outside Romanian waters, and Vladimir Putin publicly rejected the freeze-the-frontline idea that underpins the talks — all while the Oleshky humanitarian deal itself turned out to carry two different start dates.
The details, in order. According to Russia's aviation regulator Rosaviatsia, all four Moscow airports — Sheremetyevo, Domodedovo, Vnukovo and Zhukovsky — suspended arrivals and departures on Friday afternoon as air defences engaged drones approaching the capital, with restrictions published at 2:05 p.m. Moscow time. Moscow mayor Sergei Sobyanin said 17 drones were shot down heading toward the city that afternoon, on top of 155 he said targeted Moscow Oblast overnight. At Sheremetyevo, an air alert sounded and passengers were directed to shelters, and an unverified social-media image purported to show drone debris on the tarmac; the Kyiv Independent could not independently verify it. Flight trackers disagreed on the scale — one count put Sheremetyevo alone at 85 cancellations and 229 delays over the day, another put all four airports at 147 delays and 31 cancellations as of 2:31 p.m. — so treat any single tally as partial. An evacuation was also reported at the IQ-Quarter tower in Moscow City, which houses several Russian government ministries; TASS later said, citing emergency services, that alarm was false. The Institute for the Study of War (ISW) notes this was the second full closure of all four Moscow airports in two days, after a similar shutdown on October 22.
What each side argues has, if anything, hardened. Putin said on October 22 that occupied Ukraine is "the territory of historical Russia" while rejecting Zelenskyy's October 21 proposal to freeze the current frontline, according to ISW's summary of his remarks — invoking "Novorossiya," a claimed region that, on ISW's reading, stretches beyond the four illegally annexed oblasts to include Kharkiv, Dnipropetrovsk, Mykolaiv and Odesa. ISW's assessment, stated bluntly, is that Putin's remarks show the Kremlin is willing to negotiate only to accept Kyiv's surrender, not a compromise peace — that is ISW's analysis, not a neutral fact, and Moscow would frame its demands as security guarantees, not surrender terms. Zelenskyy's side, as reported Friday, is still holding the freeze-along-current-lines offer, plus demands for security guarantees and 10 years of army funding. Meanwhile the Starlink dispute stayed unresolved into the evening: ISW reports Ukrainian officials, including the General Staff and defence ministry sources, widely reported continued in-motion speed restrictions on Starlink and Starshield on October 23, with defence minister Serhii Sternenko calling the situation "ambiguous" — some units report resumption above the old limits, others still see dropouts at speeds around 100 mph, and there is, per a ministry source, "no confirmation" the restrictions have been lifted. That directly contradicts Thursday's claim that full access had been restored.
For ordinary people, the spillover is the story. Romanian president Nicusor Dan said on October 23 that an unspecified drone struck the Comoros-flagged cargo ship Khoryv near Romanian territorial waters — about 13 nautical miles off Constanta, just outside the 12-mile limit — calling it a consequence of "Russia's aggression against Ukraine"; European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen called it yet another "Russian escalation" in the Black Sea. Moldovan police separately reported drone debris falling up to 100 meters from a residential building near Chistelnica on October 23. ISW notes this follows likely Russian strikes on two tankers inside Romanian waters on October 14–15 and on civilian vessels in Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone on October 12–13 — a pattern, in ISW's view, of growing willingness to hit targets that touch NATO or NATO-aligned territory. And the Oleshky date gap matters for the 1,700–2,000 mostly elderly people still there: Gerasimov said Russian forces would cease fire on the Kherson axis from 4 a.m. Moscow time on October 27, while the White House release — and Melania Trump's own statement — put the localized ceasefire's start on October 29. Until one date is confirmed by the aid operation itself, the evacuation timetable is uncertain.
In short: Friday's talks window and prisoner swap are real, but Putin's own words point away from a frontline freeze, the Starlink limits are still reported in place, and the war disrupted Moscow air travel and Black Sea shipping on the same day. Watch for which Oleshky date the aid convoys actually run on, for any verified change in Starlink speeds, and for whether the Black Sea strikes draw a NATO response beyond statements.
Source: understandingwar.org.

The Institute for the Study of War (ISW) notes this was the second full closure of all four Moscow airports in two days, after a similar shutdown on October 22.

Putin said on October 22 that occupied Ukraine is "the territory of historical Russia" while rejecting Zelenskyy's October 21 proposal to freeze the current frontline, according to ISW's summary of his remarks — invoking "Novorossiya," a claimed region that, on ISW's reading, stretches beyond the four illegally annexed oblasts to include Kharkiv, Dnipropetrovsk, Mykolaiv and Odesa. ISW's assessment, stated bluntly, is that Putin's remarks show the Kremlin is willing to negotiate only to accept Kyiv's surrender, not a compromise peace — that is ISW's analysis, not a neutral fact, and Moscow would frame its demands as security guarantees, not surrender terms. Zelenskyy's side, as reported Friday, is still holding the freeze-along-current-lines offer, plus demands for security guarantees and 10 years of army funding. Meanwhile the Starlink dispute stayed unresolved into the evening: ISW reports Ukrainian officials, including the General Staff and defence ministry sources, widely reported continued in-motion speed restrictions on Starlink and Starshield on October 23, with defence minister Serhii Sternenko calling the situation "ambiguous" — some units report resumption above the old limits, others still see dropouts at speeds around 100 mph, and there is, per a ministry source, "no confirmation" the restrictions have been lifted. That directly contradicts Thursday's claim that full access had been restored.

For ordinary people, the spillover is the story. Romanian president Nicusor Dan said on October 23 that an unspecified drone struck the Comoros-flagged cargo ship Khoryv near Romanian territorial waters — about 13 nautical miles off Constanta, just outside the 12-mile limit — calling it a consequence of "Russia's aggression against Ukraine"; European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen called it yet another "Russian escalation" in the Black Sea. Moldovan police separately reported drone debris falling up to 100 meters from a residential building near Chistelnica on October 23. ISW notes this follows likely Russian strikes on two tankers inside Romanian waters on October 14–15 and on civilian vessels in Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone on October 12–13 — a pattern, in ISW's view, of growing willingness to hit targets that touch NATO or NATO-aligned territory. And the Oleshky date gap matters for the 1,700–2,000 mostly elderly people still there: Gerasimov said Russian forces would cease fire on the Kherson axis from 4 a.m. Moscow time on October 27, while the White House release — and Melania Trump's own statement — put the localized ceasefire's start on October 29. Until one date is confirmed by the aid operation itself, the evacuation timetable is uncertain.

In short: Friday's talks window and prisoner swap are real, but Putin's own words point away from a frontline freeze, the Starlink limits are still reported in place, and the war disrupted Moscow air travel and Black Sea shipping on the same day. Watch for which Oleshky date the aid convoys actually run on, for any verified change in Starlink speeds, and for whether the Black Sea strikes draw a NATO response beyond statements.

Source: understandingwar.org — Read the full article

item.title: Washington pulls its people out as October becomes the worst month on the water
item.description:
The sharpest Friday-night development on the Gulf front is not a new strike but a withdrawal: the United States has ordered non-emergency government staff and their families to leave Saudi Arabia, and Canada has added Dammam's airport to its avoid-all-travel list — while new Reuters data confirms October is already the worst month for Strait of Hormuz shipping attacks since records began.
The details first. According to NonRev Travel News' October 23 roundup, citing the State Department, spokesman Tommy Pigott said on X that non-emergency US government employees and family members must leave Saudi Arabia, citing Houthi attacks on civilian airports; the order applies to Saudi Arabia only, and Pigott called reports of a Gulf-wide order "inaccurate," though Reuters and AFP sources said families at some other Gulf posts are also being told to leave. The underlying reporting dates the order to October 22 — it was not in the evening brief, so it is reported here as a catch-up, not a Friday-night decision. Canada's travel advice, updated October 22, now says to avoid all travel to King Fahd International Airport in Dammam and King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh because of military activity disrupting airport operations; the overall level is unchanged at avoid non-essential travel. On the ground, Riyadh's airport has resumed only a limited number of domestic flights on Saudia and flynas, subject to prior approval, with most foreign airlines still away — which settles the evening brief's open question in favour of "partly open, not really open." Saudi aviation authority GACA says Dammam resumed operations after Wednesday night's attack, which killed two people and injured eight.
On the fighting itself, ISW's October 23 Iran update reports Saudi air defences intercepted two ballistic missiles over Riyadh and Khamis Mushait and two drones over the southern region on October 23, in addition to a missile over Najran on October 22 — coalition-side claims, as usual, without independent confirmation of what was hit or missed. In Yemen, ISW also notes Yemeni government-aligned forces repelled Houthi attempts around Taiz City's "Old Airport" neighbourhood on October 22, after similar attempts on October 17–18, and that the Houthis fully encircled the city on October 12 — a reminder the ground war in Taiz is moving even as the air war dominates headlines.
The shipping numbers are the reason this is a major article, not just a travel notice. Reuters reported Friday, from Washington Institute fellow Noam Raydan's incident map, that October has seen 28 confirmed and reported attacks in the Strait of Hormuz and surrounding waterways — the highest monthly number on record for a tracker running since 2017 — and 113 since the US-Israeli war with Iran began on February 28. The International Maritime Organization's tally broadly aligns at 120 incidents since the conflict began, with more than 30 supertankers (VLCCs) damaged, including 11 in October alone — about 3.5% of the entire global VLCC fleet. Greece-based consultancy Marisks adds that October 5–11 alone saw a dozen ships attacked, the highest weekly count of the war. Raydan's reading, via Reuters, is that Iran is intensifying attacks to slow the recovery in shipments and keep pressure on energy markets ahead of the November US midterms. Tehran's side of the argument is its claim of seven tankers hit overnight October 21–22, which President Trump publicly dismissed as fabricated, saying more oil is flowing through the Gulf than before the war; the claim remains unverified, with no vessel names given, and should not be counted as seven confirmed casualties. The US Central Command position, via Al Jazeera's reporting, is that about 95% of vessels are getting through.
For ordinary people, the costs are already concrete. Brent crude traded above $114 a barrel on Friday, a five-month peak, according to Reuters' market commentary — which is why fuel prices, not just headlines, are the transmission mechanism to watch. Airline suspensions now run deep into the calendar: Etihad and Qatar Airways suspended Riyadh and Dammam through October 24, Air France through October 24, KLM and SalamAir through October 31, Lufthansa Group through November 18 (Riyadh) and November 30 (Dammam), British Airways resuming one daily Riyadh flight only on November 3, Cathay Pacific out of Riyadh through January 31, 2027, and Delta's Atlanta–Riyadh launch postponed to March 2027. When the US pulls its own non-emergency staff, consular help for private travellers thins out too — the practical advice in the roundup is to postpone non-essential trips to Saudi Arabia.
In short: no newly verified Houthi hit on Friday night, but the US ordered departure, Canada's Dammam warning, and the record October shipping tally together say the Gulf crisis is deepening rather than stabilising. Watch for Egypt's parliament vote on military support on October 26, for any CENTCOM word on the claimed Sirik strike, and for whether Brent holds above $114 or retreats. No clean lead image could be retrieved from the Reuters or travel-roundup pages this evening, so this article runs without one rather than with a guessed image.
Source: nonrevtravelnews.com.

item.title: Wayve, Stellantis and Nvidia join France's government on an autonomous-vehicle push
item.description:
Announced October 23 at the Assises du Véhicule Autonome in Paris: Wayve's AI Driver, integrating Nvidia's Halos OS on Nvidia Hyperion compute and sensor architecture, combined with Stellantis' L4-Ready platforms and vehicle engineering, with the French government backing deployment in France and across the EU.
Wayve frames France — one of Europe's largest ride-hailing markets — as the base for a full autonomous-vehicle value chain, from chips to vehicles. Why it matters: this is a government-backed deployment pact, not just a tech demo, and it builds on existing Wayve–Stellantis–Nvidia collaborations.
Still an announcement, not cars on the road — watch for deployment dates.
Source: unite.ai.

item.title: OBS Studio 33.0.0 released October 23
item.description:
The free, open-source streaming and recording app's new stable release overhauls plugin loading (first-party plugins move to a new "core" folder; third-party plugins get a new location, with legacy locations still loading until version 34.0), improves source snapping in the preview with a new visual indicator, and runs on Windows 10+, macOS 13+ (Apple Silicon native) and Linux.
Why it matters: OBS is the default streaming tool for a huge share of creators, and a plugin-loading overhaul is the kind of change to check before upgrading mid-project.
Source: obs-versions.com.

item.title: Claude controls Photoshop via an open-source MCP server — unofficial
item.description:
An independent developer released a Photoshop MCP server on October 23 under an MIT licence on GitHub, letting Claude automate Photoshop tasks through natural-language commands via ExtendScript modules.
It needs Node.js 18+, a Claude API subscription and a licensed Photoshop copy. Flag: this is explicitly not affiliated with Anthropic or Adobe — a community project, not an official integration — so treat its roadmap (generative fill, batch processing) as aspirational.
Why it matters: it shows MCP moving from chatbots into professional creative tools.
Source: emergent.sh.

item.title: Nextcloud Collabora flaw joins CISA's exploited list — disabling the app does not protect you
item.description:
CISA added CVE-2026-110447 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on October 23, with a federal deadline of Monday, October 26.
The flaw is an unauthenticated command injection (CVSS 9.2) in Nextcloud's optional Collabora Online – Built-in CODE Server app (richdocumentscode); attackers have used it since September 10 to plant web shells and hunt for password vaults and crypto wallets, per the Carthage Electronics threat brief. The fix is version 26.4.303, and Collabora says simply disabling the app does *not* protect you.
Note: exploitation of this flaw was first reported October 15; the KEV listing and Monday deadline are what's new.
Source: carthageelectronics.com.

item.description:
From the same October 23 threat brief: the Expressway flaw reaches root in clustered deployments, and the Snort 3 bugs reach Cisco Secure Firewall.
Separately, Canada's Cyber Centre says the Redis RESTORE flaw CVE-2026-25243 is being exploited, WordPress sites running Prime Mover have an unauthenticated object-injection bug to patch, and Wiz reports the China-aligned Storm-0940 crew is aiming an AI attack agent at other software vendors. Check vendor advisories for fixed versions before acting — the brief is remediation-only by design.
Source: carthageelectronics.com.
